title: Kantian Ethics and Utilitarianism
welcome_lead: Set deontology against consequentialism: Kant's categorical imperative in conversation with Bentham's hedonic calculus and Mill's qualitative refinement.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on Kantian deontology and utilitarianism: categorical imperative, hedonic calculus, act/rule, and applications.
final_note: You have weighed Kantian and utilitarian frameworks on principle and on cases.

concepts.def: For Kant, the only thing good without qualification.
An unconditional command of reason; the moral law in formulation.
A maxim's capacity, without contradiction, to be willed as universal law.
The highest good: virtue conjoined with happiness; Kant's postulate of God and immortality follows.
Bentham's foundation: maximise pleasure and minimise pain.
Mill's qualitative distinction protecting utilitarianism from the 'doctrine of swine' charge.

walkthroughs.body_html: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason (1788) argues that the summum bonum - virtue rewarded with proportionate happiness - is the necessary object of the moral will. Since virtue cannot guarantee happiness in this life, practical reason requires three postulates: freedom (we must act), immortality (to complete moral perfection) and God (to apportion happiness to virtue).

Bentham's Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789) gives the principle of utility and the hedonic calculus. Mill's Utilitarianism (1863) introduces higher pleasures, defends utilitarianism against the swine objection, and offers his controversial 'proof' that the desirable is what is desired.

Act utilitarianism judges each act; rule utilitarianism judges rules. R. M. Hare's two-level utilitarianism distinguishes intuitive everyday rules and critical thinking for hard cases. Peter Singer defends preference utilitarianism, evaluating acts by their satisfaction or frustration of considered preferences. Bernard Williams and Bernard Hodgson criticise integrity-violation in utilitarian thinking.
